spec: Given a list of 2-element tuples, group the second elements by the first, preserving the order in which they appeared (including duplicates). Return a dict mapping each distinct first element to a list of its corresponding second elements. An empty list returns an empty dict.
Pad a string on the left with spaces so its total length equals width. If the string is already at least as long as width, return it unchanged. Width is a non-negative integer.

Given two lists of integers that are each already sorted in ascending order, conceptually merge them into one sorted list and return its median as a float, using the same odd/even averaging rule as a standard median.
Given a date string "DD-MM-YYYY" and an integer n (which may be negative), return the date string "DD-MM-YYYY" of the date n days later, correctly handling month and year boundaries and leap years.

Convert a (possibly negative) integer number of seconds into a signed clock string: the absolute value is formatted as "HH:MM:SS" (each field zero-padded to two digits, hours may exceed two digits), preceded by a "-" if the input was negative, or by nothing if it was zero or positive.
Lowercase the filename and replace every space with a hyphen, then remove any character that is not a lowercase letter, digit, hyphen, or period.

Validate a password requiring all four character classes: it must be between 8 and 64 characters long (inclusive) and contain at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one special (non-alphanumeric) character. Return False if any requirement is not met.

Write a function that finds interior 'peaks' in a list of numbers, where a peak is an element strictly greater than both of its immediate neighbors (the first and last elements can never be peaks), and returns the index of the peak with the largest value. If several peaks share the largest value, return the smallest such index. If there are no peaks, return -1.

Given a string of lowercase letters, determine whether some permutation (reordering) of its characters could form a palindrome. This is possible exactly when at most one character has an odd count of occurrences. Return True if a palindrome permutation is possible, otherwise False. An empty string is considered valid (True).

Given an integer weekday index that represents 0 = Sunday, 1 = Monday, ..., 6 = Saturday, but may be negative or 7 or greater, normalize it modulo 7 and return the full English name of the resulting weekday.
Determine whether a positive integer n is a (generalized, only-positive-index) pentagonal number, i.e. n = k*(3*k-1)/2 for some positive integer k.

Truncate a string to at most maxlen characters, replacing the final characters with '...' if truncation is needed so the result is exactly maxlen characters long. If the string already fits, return it unchanged. If maxlen is 3 or less, just hard-truncate to maxlen characters without adding an ellipsis.

Validate a binary fraction string of the form 'int.frac' where int and frac are each non-empty strings of only '0' and '1' characters, and there is exactly one '.' separating them. Return False if either side is empty, either side contains a non-binary character, or the dot is missing or duplicated.

Given a non-empty list of time strings in 'HH:MM' format, compute the average time of day by averaging the minutes-since-midnight values using integer (floor) division, and return the result formatted as an 'HH:MM' string.
Given a block of text, prefix every line (split on newline characters) with '> ' to render it as a markdown-style blockquote, then rejoin the lines with newline characters.
For a positive integer n, return the smallest power of two that is greater than or equal to n.

Count occurrences of each distinct value in items. Assign rank 1 to the most frequent value, rank 2 to the next, and so on; when several values are tied on count, break the tie by ordering them alphabetically/numerically (smaller value gets the better, i.e. lower, rank number). Return a dict mapping each distinct value to its rank.
Convert a string with words separated by spaces, hyphens, or underscores into CONSTANT_CASE: uppercase every word and join them with underscores.

Bucket each non-negative integer age into a decade label: '0-9', '10-19', ..., '90-99', or '100+' for ages 100 and above. Return a dict mapping each label that has at least one age to the count of ages in it (labels with no ages are omitted). An empty list returns an empty dict.

Given a non-empty list of scores, pair each score with its percentile rank: 100 times the count of scores less than or equal to it divided by the total, rounded to the nearest whole number. Return a list of (value, percentile) tuples, one for every input score including duplicates, sorted ascending by value.

Write a function that finds the smallest positive integer (1 or greater) that does not appear in a list of integers. The list may contain negatives, zero, duplicates, or be unordered. Return that smallest missing positive integer.
Given a string s, return a copy of s with every character that is not an alphabetic letter removed, preserving the order and original case of the remaining letters.

Given a list of strings, return them sorted according to the alphabetical order of each string reversed (compare the strings as if each were spelled backwards), but return the original (non-reversed) strings in that order. The input list may be empty.

Write a function that finds the value that forms the longest maximal run of consecutive equal elements in a list. If several runs tie for the longest length, return the value of whichever tied run occurs first. Return None for an empty list.
Given a starting weekday number (0=Monday .. 6=Sunday) and an integer number of days to advance n (which may be negative or larger than a week), return the resulting weekday number (0-6).
Given a string s, return the index of the first uppercase letter found in s, scanning left to right. Return -1 if s contains no uppercase letters, including for an empty string.

Wrap every string in the given list in double quotes, then join them into a natural-language list with commas and 'and' before the last item, following the standard oxford-comma rule (zero items give an empty string, one quoted item is returned alone, two are joined with 'and', three or more use an oxford comma).

Write a function that returns a list of suffix sums where each output element is the sum of all input elements from that position to the end of the list (inclusive). The output has the same length as the input; an empty input returns an empty output.
Return a sorted list of all keys that appear in either dict d1 or d2 (or both). If both dicts are empty, return an empty list.

Given a list of dicts with numeric values, compute for every key that appears in at least one dict the average of its value across ALL the dicts in the list, treating a dict that is missing the key as contributing 0 (so the divisor is always the total number of dicts, not just those containing the key). Round each average to 2 decimal places. An empty list returns an empty dict.
Given a list of (a, b) integer tuples, return them sorted by the sum a + b in ascending order. If two tuples have the same sum, order by the first element a ascending. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of (character, count) tuples, reconstruct and return the string formed by repeating each character the given number of times, concatenated in the order the tuples appear. A count of 0 contributes nothing to the result, and an empty list returns an empty string.
Determine whether every character in a string is distinct, meaning no character appears more than once. Case is significant, and an empty string has all unique characters by definition.
submission:
from collections import Counter

def has_all_unique_chars(s):
    counts = Counter(s)
    largest_count = max(counts.values(), default=0)
    return largest_count <= 1

spec: Given a string s and a single character ch, remove exactly the first occurrence and the last occurrence of ch from s (if ch occurs only once, remove just that single instance), leaving all other characters, including any other occurrences of ch, in place. If ch does not appear in s, return s unchanged.

Given a string, apply CSV-style quoting: if it contains a comma, a double-quote character, or a newline character, wrap it in double quotes and double any internal double-quote characters (replace each " with two ""). If none of those characters are present, return the string unchanged.

Given a list of integers, return True if the list is sorted in non-decreasing order (each element is less than or equal to the next), and False otherwise. An empty list or a single-element list is considered sorted.
Convert a camelCase string into kebab-case by inserting a hyphen before every internal uppercase letter and lowercasing the whole result.

Validate a credit-card-style string of the format 'XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX' where each X is a digit: exactly four groups of four digits separated by hyphens. Additionally the 16 digits (read without hyphens) must pass the Luhn checksum (double every second digit from the right, subtracting 9 if over 9, and the total must be divisible by 10). Return True only if both the format and the checksum are valid.
Validate a flight number string: it must consist of exactly 2 uppercase letters followed by either 3 or 4 digits, with no other characters. Return False otherwise.

Keep only the first maxwords whitespace-separated words of a string, joined by single spaces, and append '...' if there were more words than maxwords. If the string has maxwords or fewer words, return it re-joined with single spaces and no ellipsis.
visible_tests: assert truncate_words_ellipsis('the quick brown fox', 2) == 'the quick...'
assert truncate_words_ellipsis('one two three', 3) == 'one two three'
